citation: (1) Becker, Rush, Barnes, Rein (METR), 'Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity', arXiv:2507.09089, v1 12 Jul 2025, v2 25 Jul 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089 (blog: https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/). (2) Becker, Rush, Cunningham, Rein, Mahamud, 'We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design', METR blog, 24 Feb 2026, https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/
source_tier: Preprint (arXiv, no peer-reviewed venue seen) plus non-profit research organisation blog post. Institutional research, not vendor.
access_status: Re-opened 15 Oct 2026: arXiv abstract page, arXiv v2 HTML (first ~100k of 200k characters; Appendix C.2.5 full text not seen in this pass), and METR 24 Feb 2026 post (intro and 30% to 50% sentence). Remaining detail relies on the earlier report.md, which recorded the full read.

The arXiv v2 acknowledgements open 'We thank the open-source developers who participated in this study' and contain no funding statement on the portion read. METR funders not checked [uncertain].
exact_quotes: arXiv abstract: 'Before starting tasks, developers forecast that allowing AI will reduce completion time by 24%.'
arXiv abstract: 'After completing the study, developers estimate that allowing AI reduced completion time by 20%.'
arXiv abstract: 'Surprisingly, we find that allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%—AI tooling slowed developers down.'
arXiv abstract: '16 developers with moderate AI experience complete 246 tasks in mature projects'
arXiv v2 Section 4.1: 'We caution readers against overgeneralizing on the basis of our results.'

METR 24 Feb 2026, intro para 3: 'we have observed a significant increase in developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI, which likely biases downwards our estimate of AI-assisted speedup.'
METR 24 Feb 2026, intro para 5: 'Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%.'

METR 24 Feb 2026, intro para 5: 'For the subset of the original developers who participated in the later study, we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%. Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%.'
METR 24 Feb 2026, intro para 7: 'Some developers self-report very high speedups, though as we documented in our earlier study those estimates can be quite unreliable.'
METR 24 Feb 2026, body: 'When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.'
METR 24 Feb 2026, intro para 4: 'our data is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase.'
date_and_recency: 2025 trial: tasks done Feb to Jun 2025; blog 10 Jul 2025; arXiv v1 12 Jul 2025, v2 25 Jul 2025. Follow-up: experiment started Aug 2025, post dated 24 Feb 2026; public data timestamps 12 Aug 2025 to 23 Feb 2026 (own tabulation in earlier report).
key_claims: 2025: experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with early-2025 AI allowed, while believing the opposite (forecast 24% faster before, estimated 20% faster after). 2026: follow-up data are an unreliable signal because developers opted out of working without AI; METR believes developers are likely more sped up now but the data is very weak evidence; it is changing the design. METR also says developer self-reports of speedup can be quite unreliable.
headline_figures: Developer forecast before tasks: AI reduces completion time by 24%. Developer post-hoc estimate after study: AI reduced completion time by 20%. Measured: AI increases completion time by 19% (CI +2% to +39%, as stated in the Feb 2026 post). Perception gap: roughly 39 to 43 percentage points between belief (about 20% to 24% faster) and result (19% slower); this subtraction is mine, not a quoted figure. Experts forecast 39% (economics, n=34) and 38% (ML, n=54) reductions. 16 developers, 246 tasks, $150/hour. Follow-up (Aug 2025 on): 57 developers, 143 repos, 800+ tasks, $50/hour; returning developers (n=10) -18% [-38%, +9%], new developers (n=47) -4% [-15%, +9%], where negative means less time with AI; both intervals include zero. 30% to 50% of surveyed developers withheld some tasks. Note the 2026 post itself rounds the 2025 result to '20% slowdown' in sentence one and '19% longer' in para 5.
sample_unit_and_population: Task-level randomisation within developer. 2025: 16 experienced open-source developers (average 5 years on their repository), 246 issues (136 AI-allowed, 110 AI-disallowed), mature repositories, tools mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. 2026: 57 developers (10 returning, 47 new), median 10 years experience, agentic tools such as Claude Code and Codex.
observed_vs_stated: Both. Completion time is observed (self-recorded, cross-checked with screen recordings in 2025). The 24% forecast and 20% post-hoc figures are stated beliefs. The 2026 reasons for the redesign (opt-out, task withholding) rest on surveys and interviews, not a measured quantity.
what_makes_trust_justified: A randomised field experiment with robust outcome measures. The paper's discussion says the result underscores 'the importance of conducting field experiments with robust outcome measures, compared to relying solely on expert forecasts or developer surveys' (recorded in earlier report; not re-opened this pass). Developers' forecasts did track relative task length (Pearson 0.64 and 0.59) but not the effect of AI.
what_it_costs: Developers paid $150/hour (2025) and $50/hour (2026) and must forgo AI on about half their tasks. 2025 data needed 143 hours of labelled screen recordings. By 2026 the cost shows up as selection: participation and compliance fell, which METR says biases estimates. METR's later note (per earlier report) says RCTs may get more expensive as no-AI effort grows.
failure_mode_class: Over-reliance and miscalibrated self-assessment: developers believed AI sped them up when it slowed them. In 2026, measurement failure from selection out of the no-AI arm.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident. The control that exposes the miscalibration is the randomised AI-disallowed arm with recorded time. METR's listed alternatives for 2026: shorter, better-paid experiments, fixed tasks, developer-level randomisation, observational data, careful questionnaires.
limitations_stated: Authors caution against overgeneralising; slowdown does not imply AI is not useful in many settings; results are specific to the setting, tools and period; not powered for multiple comparisons on subsets; sampling of developers non-random; self-reported time. 2026 post: selection affects 'a minority share of developers and of tasks, which limits the degree of bias'; pay cut from $150 to $50 likely contributed; time measurement unreliable with concurrent agents. Several of these quotes come from the earlier report, not re-opened this pass.
counter_evidence: METR's own 2026 data point towards speedup, though intervals include zero and METR calls them very weak evidence. The 2025 blog now carries an 'out of date' banner. The +2% lower bound only just excludes zero and a hierarchical bootstrap gives somewhat wider intervals (per earlier report). Possible selection of heavy AI users out of the 2025 sample. Small sample (16 developers).
verification_status: Re-verified against opened primary sources this pass: 24% forecast, 20% post-hoc, 19% measured (arXiv abstract and v2 HTML); 16 developers and 246 tasks (abstract); v1 and v2 dates; -18% [-38%,+9%], -4% [-15%,+9%], 19% [+2%,+39%], opt-out sentence, 30% to 50% sentence, self-report unreliability sentence (METR post). Carried from earlier report.md, not re-opened this pass [uncertain]: 39%/38% expert forecasts and n, 136/110 split, $150 and $50 pay, 57 developers, 143 repos, correlations 0.64/0.59, Appendix C.2.5 text, funding. Peer-review status unchecked [uncertain].
usable_claim: In a randomised trial of 16 experienced open-source developers in early 2025, developers forecast that AI would cut completion time by 24% and afterwards estimated it had cut it by 20%, while measured completion time rose by 19%. METR later said that developers' self-reported speedups can be quite unreliable and that its follow-up data were too affected by selection to size the current effect.
do_not_use: Do not say AI makes developers slower in general or today; METR calls the 2025 results out of date. Do not present -18% as a slowdown (negative means less time with AI) or as a measured speedup (interval includes zero). Do not turn 30% to 50% into a share of developers refusing to work without AI; it is developers withholding some tasks. Do not quote the 34% raw difference or the 39 to 43 point gap as METR figures. Do not use unqualified 'developers think they are 20% faster but are 19% slower' as a population claim: 16 developers.
